vlsiverify-001:
**Key idea:** UVM (IEEE 1800.2) gives every team the same class library, the same testbench structure and the same simulation lifecycle. Verification components (UVCs) can then be reused from block to SoC level, reconfigured without editing their source, and driven by constrained-random, coverage-driven stimulus.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Problem["Ad-hoc SV testbench"]
    P1["initial blocks race each other"]
    P2["hard-coded classes, edit to change"]
    P3["every team invents its own structure"]
  end
  subgraph UVM["UVM provides"]
    U1["Phasing: build, connect, run, check, report"]
    U2["Factory overrides: swap types without editing code"]
    U3["Standard agent / env / test hierarchy"]
    U4["config_db, TLM, objections, RAL, reporting"]
  end
  P1 --> U1
  P2 --> U2
  P3 --> U3
  U3 --> U4
```

### Explanation
| Need | UVM mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Reuse across projects and levels | Standard base classes (`uvm_agent`, `uvm_env`, ...), active/passive agents |
| Change behavior without editing the TB | Factory (`type_id::create`, type/instance overrides) |
| Deterministic start-up and shutdown | Phases plus objections |
| Pass settings and interfaces down the hierarchy | `uvm_config_db` |
| Decoupled component communication | TLM ports and analysis ports |
| Stimulus as reusable, layered scenarios | Sequences, virtual sequences, sequence arbitration |
| Register verification | RAL (`uvm_reg_block`, adapters, predictors) |
| Consistent, filterable messages | `uvm_info/warning/error/fatal` with verbosity control |

- Because UVM is vendor-neutral, the same environment runs on VCS, Xcelium and Questa, and VIP from third parties plugs in.
- It separates test intent (tests, sequences) from testbench infrastructure (env, agents), so a new test is often just a new sequence plus a few overrides.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- UVM adds overhead. A tiny block with a handful of directed checks may not need a full UVM environment.
- Reuse only works when components are written for it: no hard-coded paths, and configuration delivered through config objects.

### Follow-ups
- *What came before UVM?* OVM and VMM. UVM grew mainly out of OVM and was standardized as IEEE 1800.2 in 2017.
- *Does UVM replace SystemVerilog?* No. It is a class library written in SystemVerilog.
vlsiverify-002:
**Key idea:** `uvm_component` is derived from `uvm_object`. Components are the quasi-static testbench structure: they are built once, have a parent and take part in phasing. Objects are transient data and configuration: they are created and discarded at any time, with no parent and no phases.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  OBJ["uvm_object"] --> TR["uvm_transaction"] --> SI["uvm_sequence_item"] --> SEQ["uvm_sequence_base / uvm_sequence"]
  OBJ --> RO["uvm_report_object"] --> COMP["uvm_component"]
  COMP --> D["uvm_driver"]
  COMP --> M["uvm_monitor"]
  COMP --> A["uvm_agent / uvm_env / uvm_test"]
  OBJ --> CFG["config objects, uvm_reg ..."]
```

### Explanation
| Feature | `uvm_object` | `uvm_component` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifetime | Dynamic: created and garbage-collected any time | Quasi-static: built in `build_phase`, lives for the whole simulation |
| Constructor | `new(string name = "...")` | `new(string name, uvm_component parent)` |
| Hierarchy | None (`get_full_name()` returns just the name) | Parent/child tree under `uvm_top` |
| Phasing | No phase methods | `build_phase`, `run_phase`, `report_phase`, ... |
| Factory macro | `` `uvm_object_utils `` | `` `uvm_component_utils `` |
| Overrides | Type override; instance override only through a context string | Type and instance override by hierarchical path |
| Examples | sequence items, sequences, config objects, register models | driver, monitor, sequencer, agent, scoreboard, env, test |

```systemverilog
class pkt extends uvm_sequence_item;
  `uvm_object_utils(pkt)
  function new(string name = "pkt"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

class my_drv extends uvm_driver #(pkt);
  `uvm_component_utils(my_drv)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- You cannot create a component after `build_phase` (end of elaboration). Creating one in `run_phase` is an error.
- Sequences are objects even though they "run". They borrow a component context through `m_sequencer`.

### Follow-ups
- *Why does a component need a parent?* The parent places it in the hierarchy. That position drives phasing order, config_db scoping and instance overrides.
- *Which class sits between them?* `uvm_report_object`, which gives components their reporting methods.

**Key idea:** `uvm_sequence_item` extends `uvm_transaction` and adds everything an item needs to travel through a sequencer: the parent sequence, the sequencer handle, and sequence/transaction IDs for routing responses. User stimulus should always extend `uvm_sequence_item`. ```mermaid flowchart LR O["uvm_object
copy, compare, print, pack"] --> T["uvm_transaction
begin_tr / end_tr, timestamps, recording, transaction_id"] T --> S["uvm_sequence_item
get_sequencer, get_parent_sequence, set_id_info, sequence_id"] S --> U["my_pkt (user item)"] ``` ### Explanation | | `uvm_transaction` | `uvm_sequence_item` | | --- | --- | --- | | Parent | `uvm_object` | `uvm_transaction` | | Adds | Transaction timing (`accept_tr`, `begin_tr`, `end_tr`), recording, events | `m_sequencer`, `m_parent_sequence`, `sequence_id`, `set_id_info()`, `get_full_name()` with the sequence path | | Can go through `start_item` / `finish_item`? | No | Yes | | Typical use | Rarely extended directly in modern code | All user stimulus and response items | - The driver must copy the IDs onto any response (`rsp.set_id_info(req)`), so the sequencer can route the response back to the sequence that issued the request. - Analysis-only items, such as a monitor's output, still usually extend `uvm_sequence_item`. That keeps one item type for both stimulus and observation. ```systemverilog class bus_item extends uvm_sequence_item; rand bit [31:0] addr, data; rand bit write; `uvm_object_utils_begin(bus_item) `uvm_field_int(addr, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_field_int(data, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_field_int(write, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_object_utils_end function new(string name = "bus_item"); super.new(name); endfunction endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - An item extending `uvm_transaction` cannot be parameterized into `uvm_sequence #(T)` or `uvm_driver #(T)`, because those require a `uvm_sequence_item`. - The UVM documentation advises against extending `uvm_transaction` directly in user code. ### Follow-ups - *Is `uvm_sequence` also a sequence item?* Yes. `uvm_sequence_base` extends `uvm_sequence_item`, which is why sequences can be nested and arbitrated on a sequencer.

**Key idea:** `new()` is the plain SystemVerilog constructor and always builds the exact type written in the code. `type_id::create()` asks the UVM factory first, so a registered override can substitute a derived class without touching the original code. ```mermaid flowchart TD C["drv = my_drv::type_id::create('drv', this)"] --> F{"Factory: override for my_drv
at this path?"} F -->|"instance override"| I["construct err_drv for this path only"] F -->|"type override"| T["construct err_drv everywhere"] F -->|"none"| N["construct my_drv"] NW["drv = new('drv', this)"] --> X["always my_drv, factory bypassed"] ``` ### Explanation | | `new()` | `type_id::create()` | | --- | --- | --- | | Defined by | SystemVerilog language | `` `uvm_*_utils `` macro (static method of the type proxy) | | Override aware | No | Yes (type and instance overrides) | | Needs factory registration | No | Yes | | Use for | Ports/exports, TLM FIFOs, `uvm_event`, plain helper classes | Components, sequences, sequence items, config objects | ```systemverilog // in the test: swap the driver without editing env/agent code function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); super.build_phase(phase); my_drv::type_id::set_type_override(err_drv::get_type()); env = my_env::type_id::create("env", this); endfunction // in the agent drv = my_drv::type_id::create("drv", this); // returns an err_drv ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The override must be registered **before** `create()` runs. In practice that means in the test's `build_phase`, before the env is created. - The override type must derive from the original type, or the factory reports an error. - `create()` still calls `new()` internally. The class needs a constructor with the standard signature. ### Follow-ups - *Is `create()` virtual?* No. It is a static method of the type proxy (`type_id`). The factory picks the actual type to construct.
vlsiverify-005:
**Key idea:** `copy()` fills an object that **already exists** with another object's field values. `clone()` **allocates a new object** with `create()`, then calls `copy()` into it. It returns a `uvm_object` handle, so you `$cast` the result.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User code
  participant S as src item
  participant D as dst item
  Note over U,D: copy()
  U->>D: dst = my_item::type_id::create("dst")
  U->>D: dst.copy(src)
  D->>S: read fields via do_copy
  Note over U,D: clone()
  U->>S: src.clone()
  S->>S: create() new object of same type
  S->>S: new_obj.copy(this)
  S-->>U: uvm_object handle
  U->>U: $cast(dst, handle)
```

### Explanation
| | `copy(rhs)` | `clone()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allocates memory | No, the destination must exist | Yes |
| Return value | `void` (function) | `uvm_object` |
| Needs `$cast` | No | Yes |
| Can be overridden | Override `do_copy()`, not `copy()` | `clone()` is virtual but rarely overridden |

```systemverilog
my_item a, b, c;
a = my_item::type_id::create("a");
void'(a.randomize());

b = my_item::type_id::create("b");
b.copy(a);                 // b already allocated

if (!$cast(c, a.clone()))  // c is a new, independent object
  `uvm_fatal("CAST", "clone cast failed")

// custom deep copy hook
virtual function void do_copy(uvm_object rhs);
  my_item r;
  super.do_copy(rhs);
  $cast(r, rhs);
  addr = r.addr;
  data = r.data;
  payload = r.payload;      // a dynamic array is copied by value
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- How deep the copy goes depends on `do_copy()` or the field macros. `uvm_field_object` with `UVM_DEEP` (the default) copies nested objects, while `UVM_REFERENCE` copies only the handle.
- Calling `copy()` on a null destination gives a null-handle runtime error.
- A monitor should send a clone, or a freshly created item, to analysis ports. That way the scoreboard never sees later mutations.

### Follow-ups
- *Can you clone a component?* No. `uvm_component::clone()` reports an error, because components cannot be duplicated.

**Key idea:** **Severity** says how serious a message is (INFO, WARNING, ERROR, FATAL) and decides the default action. **Verbosity** applies only to `UVM_INFO` and decides whether the message prints at all, compared against the component's verbosity threshold.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  M["uvm_info(ID, msg, UVM_HIGH)"] --> C{"message verbosity <= threshold?"}
  C -->|"yes"| P["print"]
  C -->|"no"| D["drop silently"]
  E["uvm_error(ID, msg)"] --> A["always processed: UVM_DISPLAY | UVM_COUNT"]
  F["uvm_fatal(ID, msg)"] --> X["UVM_DISPLAY | UVM_EXIT: ends simulation"]
```

### Explanation
| Severity | Default action | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UVM_INFO` | `UVM_DISPLAY` | Informational, filtered by verbosity |
| `UVM_WARNING` | `UVM_DISPLAY` | Unexpected but not a failure |
| `UVM_ERROR` | `UVM_DISPLAY \| UVM_COUNT` | Check failed. Simulation stops after `max_quit_count` errors (if set) |
| `UVM_FATAL` | `UVM_DISPLAY \| UVM_EXIT` | Unrecoverable failure, exits immediately |

| Verbosity | Value | Prints when threshold is `UVM_MEDIUM` (default)? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UVM_NONE` | 0 | Always |
| `UVM_LOW` | 100 | Yes |
| `UVM_MEDIUM` | 200 | Yes |
| `UVM_HIGH` | 300 | No |
| `UVM_FULL` | 400 | No |
| `UVM_DEBUG` | 500 | No |

```systemverilog
`uvm_info("DRV", $sformatf("sent %s", req.convert2string()), UVM_HIGH)
`uvm_error("SCB", "data mismatch")
// change threshold for one subtree
env.agt.set_report_verbosity_level_hier(UVM_DEBUG);
// or on the command line: +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_HIGH
// per component/ID: +uvm_set_verbosity=uvm_test_top.env.*,DRV,UVM_FULL,run
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Verbosity has no effect on warnings, errors and fatals. To change those, use `set_report_severity_action` or `set_report_severity_override`, for example to demote a known error.
- The macros check verbosity **before** evaluating `$sformatf`, so filtered messages cost almost nothing. A direct call to `uvm_report_info` does not skip that work.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you stop after N errors?* Use `+UVM_MAX_QUIT_COUNT=N` or `set_report_max_quit_count(N)`.

**Key idea:** A **sequence** is a transient object that *generates* items in its `body()`. A **sequencer** is a permanent component that *arbitrates* between running sequences and hands the granted items to the driver. ```mermaid flowchart LR S1["seq A (uvm_object)
body: start_item / finish_item"] --> SQR S2["seq B (uvm_object)"] --> SQR SQR["sequencer (uvm_component)
arbitration queue, FIFO / priority / random"] -->|"seq_item_export"| DRV["driver: seq_item_port.get_next_item"] DRV --> DUT["DUT pins"] ``` ### Explanation | | Sequence (`uvm_sequence #(REQ,RSP)`) | Sequencer (`uvm_sequencer #(REQ,RSP)`) | | --- | --- | --- | | Base | `uvm_sequence_item` → `uvm_object` | `uvm_component` | | Lifetime | Created, started, finished, discarded | Built once in `build_phase` | | Role | Stimulus *content*: what items, in what order, with what constraints | Stimulus *routing*: who goes next, response routing | | Key methods | `body()`, `start()`, `start_item()`, `finish_item()`, `lock()`, `grab()` | `set_arbitration()`, `stop_sequences()`, `seq_item_export` | | Count | Many, possibly concurrent or nested | One per agent (plus optional virtual sequencer) | ```systemverilog // test or virtual sequence wr_seq w = wr_seq::type_id::create("w"); rd_seq r = rd_seq::type_id::create("r"); fork w.start(env.agt.sqr); // both run on the same sequencer, r.start(env.agt.sqr); // the sequencer interleaves their items join ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A sequence must be started on a sequencer (`start(sqr)`), or `start_item()` fails because `m_sequencer` is null. - The sequencer grants on item boundaries. A sequence that needs back-to-back items uses `lock()` or `grab()`. ### Follow-ups - *Can a sequence run without a driver?* A virtual sequence runs on a virtual sequencer, or on `null`, and only starts child sequences. It never calls `start_item` itself.

**Key idea:** Call `run_test()` from the top module's `initial` block. Pass the test name either as a hard-coded argument or, preferably, with `+UVM_TESTNAME=<test>` at runtime, so one compiled image can run every test.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  TOP["tb_top: initial run_test()"] --> Q{"+UVM_TESTNAME given?"}
  Q -->|"yes"| N["use plusarg name (overrides the argument)"]
  Q -->|"no"| A{"argument given?"}
  A -->|"yes"| AN["use run_test('name')"]
  A -->|"no"| E["fatal: no test specified"]
  N --> F["factory creates uvm_test_top"]
  AN --> F
  F --> PH["phases: build ... final"]
  PH --> FIN["$finish (finish_on_completion)"]
```

### Solution
```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  `include "uvm_macros.svh"
  import my_test_pkg::*;          // makes test classes visible to the factory

  bit clk;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;
  dut_if vif(clk);
  dut    u_dut(.clk(clk), .data(vif.data) /* ... */);

  initial begin
    uvm_config_db#(virtual dut_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.*", "vif", vif);
    run_test();                    // test chosen by +UVM_TESTNAME
  end
endmodule
```

```bash
# compile once, run many tests
xrun -uvm -f files.f +UVM_TESTNAME=smoke_test  +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_LOW
xrun -uvm -f files.f +UVM_TESTNAME=stress_test +ntb_random_seed=1234
```

| Method | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run_test("smoke_test")` | Simple for a single test | Recompile or edit to change tests |
| `run_test()` + `+UVM_TESTNAME` | One build runs all tests, works with regressions | Name must match a registered class exactly |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The test class must be registered with `` `uvm_component_utils `` and compiled into the image. Otherwise the factory cannot find it ("Requested test from command line +UVM_TESTNAME=... not found").
- If both are given, the plusarg wins.

### Follow-ups
- *What is the test instance called?* `uvm_test_top`, a child of `uvm_top`.
vlsiverify-010:
**Key idea:** A sequence is a factory-registered `uvm_object` whose `body()` repeatedly runs the item handshake: create, `start_item` (wait for a grant), randomize late, `finish_item` (wait for `item_done`).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SEQ as my_sequence.body
  participant SQR as sequencer
  participant DRV as driver
  SEQ->>SQR: start_item(req) requests a grant
  DRV->>SQR: get_next_item()
  SQR-->>SEQ: grant (start_item returns)
  SEQ->>SEQ: req.randomize() late randomization
  SEQ->>SQR: finish_item(req)
  SQR-->>DRV: req
  DRV->>DRV: drive pins
  DRV->>SQR: item_done()
  SQR-->>SEQ: finish_item returns
```

### Code
```systemverilog
class my_sequence extends uvm_sequence #(my_seq_item);   // (1) REQ type sets req/rsp handles
  `uvm_object_utils(my_sequence)                          // (2) factory registration (object)

  rand int unsigned num_items = 10;                       // (3) knob, randomizable by the parent
  constraint c_num { num_items inside {[1:50]}; }

  function new(string name = "my_sequence");              // (4) object constructor: name only
    super.new(name);
  endfunction

  virtual task body();                                    // (5) the stimulus lives here
    repeat (num_items) begin
      req = my_seq_item::type_id::create("req");          // (6) factory create: overridable
      start_item(req);                                    // (7) arbitrate, wait for driver
      if (!req.randomize() with { addr < 32'h100; })      // (8) late randomization
        `uvm_error(get_type_name(), "randomize failed")
      finish_item(req);                                   // (9) send, block until item_done
      `uvm_info(get_type_name(), req.convert2string(), UVM_HIGH)
    end
  endtask
endclass

// usage (in a test's run_phase)
// my_sequence seq = my_sequence::type_id::create("seq");
// phase.raise_objection(this);
// if (!seq.randomize()) `uvm_fatal("TEST", "seq randomize")
// seq.start(env.agt.sqr);
// phase.drop_objection(this);
```

### Explanation
- `req` and `rsp` are inherited members typed from the class parameters, so there is no need to redeclare them. A local `my_seq_item req;` would shadow them.
- Randomizing after `start_item` lets constraints depend on state that exists only at grant time.
- `finish_item` returns once the driver calls `item_done()`. If a response is expected, call `get_response(rsp)` next.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use `` `uvm_object_utils ``, not `` `uvm_component_utils ``. A sequence is an object.
- Forgetting `item_done()` in the driver hangs `finish_item` forever.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not `` `uvm_do ``?* Explicit calls are easier to debug and allow custom randomization or error handling.
vlsiverify-011:
**Key idea:** Monitors publish observed transactions on `uvm_analysis_port`s. The scoreboard receives them through `uvm_analysis_imp`s, which call its `write_*()` functions, or through `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo`s that it drains in `run_phase`. The env wires everything up in `connect_phase`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph IN["input agent"]
    IM["in_mon.ap"]
  end
  subgraph OUT["output agent"]
    OM["out_mon.ap"]
  end
  IM -->|"write"| RM["reference model / predictor"]
  RM -->|"expected"| EF["scb.exp_fifo (uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo)"]
  OM -->|"actual"| AF["scb.act_fifo (uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo)"]
  EF --> CMP["scb.run_phase: get both, compare"]
  AF --> CMP
  IM -->|"write"| COV["coverage subscriber"]
```

### Explanation
**Option A: analysis imps (callback style)**
```systemverilog
`uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_exp)
`uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_act)
class my_scb extends uvm_scoreboard;
  uvm_analysis_imp_exp #(pkt, my_scb) exp_imp;
  uvm_analysis_imp_act #(pkt, my_scb) act_imp;
  pkt q[$];
  function void write_exp(pkt t); q.push_back(t); endfunction
  function void write_act(pkt t);
    pkt e;
    if (q.size() == 0) begin `uvm_error("SCB", "unexpected output") return; end
    e = q.pop_front();
    if (!t.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", "mismatch")
  endfunction
  // new(): create exp_imp / act_imp with new("exp_imp", this)
endclass
```
**Option B: analysis FIFOs (thread style)**
```systemverilog
uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(pkt) exp_fifo, act_fifo;   // built with new("exp_fifo", this)
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  pkt e, a;
  forever begin
    act_fifo.get(a);
    exp_fifo.get(e);
    if (!a.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", "mismatch")
  end
endtask
```
**Connection in the env**
```systemverilog
function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  in_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.exp_imp);            // A
  out_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.act_fifo.analysis_export); // B
  in_agt.mon.ap.connect(cov.analysis_export);    // same port fans out to many
endfunction
```

| | `uvm_analysis_imp` | `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Receives in | `write()` function (zero time) | Unbounded FIFO, then `get()` in a task |
| Multiple inputs | Needs `` `uvm_analysis_imp_decl `` suffixes | One FIFO per stream, no macros |
| Good for | Simple, in-order, immediate checks | Checks that wait or align two streams in time |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `write()` is a function and cannot block or wait.
- The monitor must send a new object each time (create or clone). Otherwise every queued entry points at the same, mutating item.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you check that nothing is left over?* In `check_phase`, report an error if the expected queue or FIFO is not empty (`exp_fifo.is_empty()`).

**Key idea:** The graceful way to end is to let all objections drop, so UVM runs extract, check, report and final and then calls `$finish`. The other exits (`uvm_fatal`, max-quit-count, global timeout, `$finish`) end abruptly. Some still print a report summary, while `$finish` skips everything.

```mermaid
  A -->|"all objections dropped"| G["extract, check, report, final, then $finish"]
  A -->|"uvm_fatal or max_quit_count reached"| F["UVM_EXIT: report summary printed, die"]
  A -->|"global timeout (set_timeout)"| T["fatal PH_TIMEOUT: phase hung"]
  A -->|"$finish / $stop in user code"| X["immediate stop, no check or report"]
  A -->|"phase.jump / uvm_domain::jump_all"| J["skip to a later phase, e.g. extract"]
```

| Mechanism | Cleanup phases run? | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drop all objections | Yes | Normal test end |
| `` `uvm_fatal(ID, msg) `` | No (`die()` prints the report summary) | Unrecoverable condition (missing vif, bad config) |
| `+UVM_MAX_QUIT_COUNT=N` / `set_report_max_quit_count(N)` | No (summary only) | Stop after N errors in regressions |
| `uvm_top.set_timeout(t)` / `+UVM_TIMEOUT=t` | No (fatal) | Watchdog against hangs |

| `$finish` | No | Avoid in UVM code |

**Key idea:** The sequence and driver never talk directly. The sequence asks the sequencer for a grant (`start_item`) and hands over the item (`finish_item`). The driver pulls items through its `seq_item_port` (`get_next_item`) and signals completion (`item_done`), which unblocks the sequence. Optional responses flow back by sequence ID.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SEQ as sequence
  participant SQR as sequencer
  participant DRV as driver
  DRV->>SQR: get_next_item(req) (blocks, driver ready)
  SEQ->>SQR: start_item(req) (request arbitration)
  SQR-->>SEQ: grant, start_item returns
  SEQ->>SEQ: randomize req (late)
  SEQ->>SQR: finish_item(req)
  SQR-->>DRV: get_next_item returns req
  DRV->>DRV: drive req on vif
  DRV->>SQR: item_done(rsp optional)
  SQR-->>SEQ: finish_item returns
  SEQ->>SQR: get_response(rsp) optional
```

### Explanation
**Connection (agent `connect_phase`)**
```systemverilog
drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export);
```
**Driver loop**
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  forever begin
    seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
    drive(req);                              // pin wiggling, consumes time
    rsp = my_item::type_id::create("rsp");
    rsp.set_id_info(req);                    // route response to the right sequence
    rsp.rdata = vif.rdata;
    seq_item_port.item_done(rsp);            // or item_done() with no response
  end
endtask
```
**Sequence**
```systemverilog
task body();
  req = my_item::type_id::create("req");
  start_item(req);
  void'(req.randomize());
  finish_item(req);
  get_response(rsp);                         // only if driver returns one
endtask
```
| Side | Blocking call | Unblocked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sequence `start_item` | waits for grant | Sequencer arbitration plus driver request |
| Sequence `finish_item` | waits for completion | Driver `item_done()` |
| Driver `get_next_item` | waits for an item | Sequence `finish_item` |

- If `item_done()` is never called, the sequence hangs in `finish_item`. Calling `get_next_item()` twice without `item_done()` is an error.

- *Alternative driver style?* `get(req)` followed by `put(rsp)`. Here `get` performs the `item_done` implicitly.

**Key idea:** `lock()` and `grab()` both give one sequence exclusive use of a sequencer until `unlock()` / `ungrab()`. **lock** joins the back of the arbitration queue and waits its turn. **grab** jumps to the front and takes effect at the next arbitration, right after the current item finishes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as seq A (running)
  participant B as seq B (waiting)
  participant L as seq L (lock)
  participant G as seq G (grab)
  participant Q as sequencer
  A->>Q: item A1 in progress
  B->>Q: start_item queued
  L->>Q: lock() queued behind B
  G->>Q: grab() put at FRONT
  Q-->>G: granted after A1 completes
  G->>Q: G1, G2, G3 back-to-back
  G->>Q: ungrab()
  Q-->>B: B1 (B was ahead of L in queue)
  Q-->>L: lock granted
  L->>Q: L1, L2 back-to-back
  L->>Q: unlock()
```

### Explanation
| | `lock(sqr)` | `grab(sqr)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queue position | Back of arbitration queue | Front of queue |
| Granted when | Its turn comes under the arbitration mode | Next arbitration (after the current item) |
| Release | `unlock()` | `ungrab()` |
| Blocking? | Yes, until granted | Yes, until granted |
| Use for | Atomic multi-item transfer that can wait (a register read-modify-write sequence) | Urgent traffic such as an interrupt service sequence |

```systemverilog
task body();
  lock(m_sequencer);              // or grab(m_sequencer)
  repeat (4) begin
    req = my_item::type_id::create("req");
    start_item(req);
    void'(req.randomize() with { burst == 1; });
    finish_item(req);
  end
  unlock(m_sequencer);            // always release
endtask
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Child sequences of the locking sequence can still use the sequencer, but unrelated sequences cannot.
- A grab or lock that is never released starves every other sequence, and the test hangs.
- If the sequencer is already locked, a grab waits until that lock is released. Grabs do not pre-empt existing locks.
- `is_blocked()` / `has_lock()` let you query the state.

### Follow-ups
- *Alternative without exclusivity?* Raise the sequence priority with arbitration `UVM_SEQ_ARB_STRICT_FIFO`. Items can still interleave, though.

**Key idea:** An **in-order** scoreboard expects outputs in the same order as the inputs, so a FIFO (`push_back` / `pop_front`) is enough. An **out-of-order** scoreboard is needed when the DUT can reorder outputs (multiple channels, AXI IDs, caches, arbiters). It stores expected items keyed by an ID or tag (an associative array) and matches each actual item by its key.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph IO["In-order"]
    I1["expected queue: A B C"] --> I2["actual A: pop_front A, match"]
    I2 --> I3["actual B: pop_front B, match"]
  end
  subgraph OOO["Out-of-order"]
    O1["exp[id]: id1=A id2=B id3=C"] --> O2["actual id3=C: exp.exists(3), match, delete"]
    O2 --> O3["actual id1=A: match, delete"]
  end
```

### Explanation
| | In-order | Out-of-order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data structure | Queue / TLM FIFO | Associative array (key: ID, address, tag), or queue + search |
| Match rule | Head of queue | Lookup by key |
| DUT examples | FIFO, pipeline, single-channel UART | AXI with IDs, NoC, crossbar, multi-port memory, packet switch |
| Error detection | Order and data errors | Data errors; order errors only within a key |

```systemverilog
// out-of-order: key by transaction ID, allow several per ID
pkt exp_q[int][$];
function void write_exp(pkt t); exp_q[t.id].push_back(t); endfunction
function void write_act(pkt t);
  pkt e;
  if (!exp_q.exists(t.id) || exp_q[t.id].size() == 0) begin
    `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("unexpected id %0d", t.id)) return;
  end
  e = exp_q[t.id].pop_front();          // in-order within one ID (AXI rule)
  if (!t.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", "data mismatch")
  if (exp_q[t.id].size() == 0) exp_q.delete(t.id);
endfunction
function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  if (exp_q.num() != 0) `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("%0d ids never completed", exp_q.num()))
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using an out-of-order scoreboard on an in-order DUT hides ordering bugs. Match the checker to the spec.
- Items with no unique key (identical payloads) need a search-and-remove-first-match strategy.
- Always check for leftovers at end of test. A dropped packet is otherwise silent.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you add a latency check?* Timestamp the expected item on insert and compare `$time` at match against the allowed maximum.

**Key idea:** `uvm_barrier` is a rendezvous point. Each process calls `wait_for()` and blocks until the **threshold** number of processes have arrived, then all are released together. Use it to align independent threads (agents, sequences) at a common point.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",          "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "thread A",     "wave": "0=.....=.", "data": ["waiting","go"] },
  { "name": "thread B",     "wave": "0..=...=.", "data": ["waiting","go"] },
  { "name": "thread C",     "wave": "0......=.", "data": ["arrives+go"] },
  { "name": "waiters (thr=3)", "wave": "2=.=...2.", "data": ["0","1","2","0"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "all three released when the 3rd thread calls wait_for()" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog

// or b.set_threshold(3);

fork
  begin : a  cfg_seq.start(apb_sqr);  b.wait_for(); traffic_a.start(sqr_a); end
  begin : bb init_mem();              b.wait_for(); traffic_b.start(sqr_b); end
  begin : c  wait_link_up();          b.wait_for(); traffic_c.start(sqr_c); end

```
| Method | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `new(name, threshold)` / `set_threshold(n)` | Number of waiters needed |
| `wait_for()` | Block until threshold reached |
| `reset(wakeup = 1)` | Reset count, optionally releasing waiters |
| `set_auto_reset(1)` | Reset automatically after each release (default on), so it can be reused |

| `cancel()` | Remove one waiter |

- If fewer than threshold processes ever arrive, everyone deadlocks. Pair it with a timeout or watchdog.
- Lowering the threshold below the current waiter count with `set_threshold` releases them immediately.

- *Barrier vs `uvm_event`?* An event is one-to-many notification (`trigger` / `wait_trigger`). A barrier is many-to-many with a count.

**Key idea:** Start from the spec and a reviewed **verification plan**, build a reusable testbench, bring up with sanity tests, close features with directed plus constrained-random tests, then drive coverage and regression to closure. Sign-off is a **measured** decision: the plan is fully covered, coverage targets are met with waivers reviewed, regressions are clean, and there are no open critical bugs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1. Spec study + design/arch reviews, Q&A with designers"] --> B["2. Verification plan: features, checks, coverage model, stimulus, TB architecture"]
  B --> C["3. Build TB: agents, scoreboard/ref model, RAL, SVA, coverage"]
  C --> D["4. Bring-up: reset, register access, smoke tests"]
  D --> E["5. Feature tests: directed + constrained random, error injection"]
  E --> F["6. Regressions: many seeds, triage, bug tracking"]
  F --> G["7. Coverage analysis: code + functional + assertion, close holes"]
  G -->|"holes or new bugs"| E
  G --> H{"Sign-off criteria met?"}
  H -->|"no"| E
  H -->|"yes"| I["8. Sign-off review, hand-off to SoC (reuse agents passive)"]
```

### Explanation
| Sign-off criterion | Typical target |
| --- | --- |
| Verification plan items | 100% implemented and passing, reviewed with design and architecture |
| Functional coverage | 100% of planned covergroups and cover properties (exclusions justified) |
| Code coverage | Line/branch/condition/FSM/toggle about 95-100%, all holes reviewed and waived |
| Assertions | All pass, cover properties hit |
| Regression | N consecutive clean nightly runs, stable pass rate, no new bugs found |
| Bug status | No open P1/P2 bugs. Bug-discovery rate has flattened |
| Reviews | TB code review, test plan review, waiver review signed off |

- **Day 1 actions:** read the spec and list ambiguities, identify interfaces and protocols (reuse VIP), define the scoreboard strategy, write the plan with traceable feature IDs, and agree on milestones with design (RTL drops vs TB readiness).
- **Metrics over time:** track the bug-find rate, coverage trend and pass rate. A flat bug curve plus closed coverage is the signal to sign off.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- 100% coverage of a weak coverage model is not sign-off. The plan itself must be reviewed.
- RTL changes after sign-off (ECOs) need a delta regression and coverage re-check.
- Do not forget clock/reset variants, low-power modes, configuration parameters and CDC/lint/formal results as part of the sign-off package.

### Follow-ups
- *What if coverage is stuck at 97%?* Analyze holes: unreachable (waive with design approval), constraint gap (write directed or targeted tests), or a design bug.

**Key idea:** TLM ports and exports connect **testbench components to each other**, never the testbench to the DUT; the DUT is reached only through virtual interfaces. A **port** is the initiator side: it calls methods such as `put`, `get` or `write`. An **export** passes the call down the hierarchy, and an **imp** is the end point that actually implements the method. The legal connection chain is port → (port) → (export) → imp.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph AGT["agent"]
    subgraph PROD["producer"]
      PP["put_port"]
    end
    AP["agent.put_port (port, pass-up)"]
  end
  subgraph ENV2["consumer_wrapper"]
    EX["put_export (export, pass-down)"]
    subgraph CONS["consumer"]
      IMP["put_imp: task put()"]
    end
  end
  PP -->|"port to port: child to parent"| AP
  AP -->|"port to export"| EX
  EX -->|"export to imp"| IMP
```

### Explanation
| Object | Role | Connect rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uvm_*_port #(T)` | Calls the method (required interface) | `port.connect(port_of_parent / export / imp)` |
| `uvm_*_export #(T)` | Forwards the call into a sub-component (provided interface) | `export.connect(export_of_child / imp)` |
| `uvm_*_imp #(T, IMP)` | Ends the chain. Calls `IMP::put()` etc. | Leaf, never connects onward |

```systemverilog
class producer extends uvm_component;
  `uvm_component_utils(producer)
  uvm_blocking_put_port #(pkt) put_port;
  function new(string n, uvm_component p); super.new(n, p); put_port = new("put_port", this); endfunction
  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    pkt t = pkt::type_id::create("t");
    phase.raise_objection(this);
    void'(t.randomize());
    put_port.put(t);                    // executes consumer.put()
    phase.drop_objection(this);
  endtask
endclass

class consumer extends uvm_component;
  `uvm_component_utils(consumer)
  uvm_blocking_put_imp #(pkt, consumer) put_imp;
  function new(string n, uvm_component p); super.new(n, p); put_imp = new("put_imp", this); endfunction
  task put(pkt t);                      // the implementation
    `uvm_info("CONS", t.convert2string(), UVM_LOW)
    #10ns;                              // blocking put may consume time
  endtask
endclass

class env extends uvm_env;
  producer prod; consumer cons;
  function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    prod.put_port.connect(cons.put_imp);   // always call connect on the initiator side
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `connect()` is always called on the **initiator side** (`port.connect(export)`), never the reverse.
- An unconnected port, or connecting incompatible interfaces (blocking port to a non-blocking imp), is an elaboration error.
- One component with two imps of the same interface needs `` `uvm_blocking_put_imp_decl(_a) `` style suffixes.

### Follow-ups
- *Analysis port vs put port?* An analysis port broadcasts with a non-blocking `write()` to 0..N imps. A put port goes to exactly one imp and may block.

**Key idea:** **Analysis** ports/FIFOs are for *observation*: a one-to-many broadcast with a non-blocking `write()` function and no back-pressure, used from monitors to scoreboards and coverage. **TLM** ports/FIFOs (put/get/peek) are for *point-to-point flow control*: one producer to one consumer, possibly blocking, with a bounded FIFO. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph AN["Analysis path (observation)"] MON["monitor.ap"] -->|"write()"| AF["uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo

With two streams (expected and actual), the scoreboard needs to *wait* for the matching item. Analysis FIFOs buffer each stream, and a `run_phase` thread does blocking `get()`s to pair them. ```systemverilog class scb extends uvm_scoreboard; `uvm_component_utils(scb) uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(pkt) in_f, out_f; function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); in_f = new("in_f", this); out_f = new("out_f", this); endfunction task run_phase(uvm_phase phase); pkt i, o; forever begin in_f.get(i); // blocks until input observed out_f.get(o); // blocks until DUT output observed if (!o.compare(predict(i))) `uvm_error("SCB", "mismatch") end endtask endclass // env: in_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.in_f.analysis_export); // out_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.out_f.analysis_export); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - An analysis FIFO never applies back-pressure, so a stalled consumer grows it without bound. **Key idea:** A **sequence item** is *one* transaction (data plus constraints), for example a single bus write. A **sequence** is a *scenario generator*: its `body()` creates, randomizes and sends many items, or starts other sequences, in a particular order through a sequencer.

```mermaid
    B["body()"] --> I1["item: WR addr=0x10"]
    B --> I2["item: WR addr=0x14"]
    B --> I3["item: RD addr=0x10"]

  I2 --> SQR
  I3 --> SQR
```

| --- | --- | --- |
| Base class | `uvm_sequence_item` | `uvm_sequence #(REQ, RSP)` (also derived from `uvm_sequence_item`) |
| Represents | One transaction | An ordered or random series of items or sub-sequences |
| Contains | `rand` fields, constraints, copy/compare/print | `body()` task, knobs, possibly constraints |
| Started by | `start_item` / `finish_item` inside a sequence | `seq.start(sequencer)` |
| Consumed by | Driver | Never reaches the driver itself |

```systemverilog
  rand bit        write;
  constraint c_al { addr[1:0] == 0; }
  `uvm_object_utils(bus_item)
  function new(string name = "bus_item"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

    bit [31:0] a;
```

- *Is `finish_item` blocking?* Yes, until `item_done`. In a pipelined driver it can return before the transfer completes on the bus.
artofverif-013:
**Key idea:** Normally the sequencer arbitrates **per item**, so items from concurrent sequences interleave. A sequence gets exclusive access with **`lock()`**/**`unlock()`**, which queues behind existing requests and waits its turn, or with **`grab()`**/**`ungrab()`**, which jumps to the front of the queue and wins the next arbitration. Either way, only that sequence (and its children) can send items until it releases.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant N as normal_seq
  participant X as atomic_seq
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant D as driver
  N->>Q: item N0
  Q->>D: N0
  X->>Q: lock() (waits for slot)
  Q-->>X: lock granted
  X->>Q: X0
  Q->>D: X0
  N->>Q: item N1 (blocked: sequencer locked)
  X->>Q: X1
  Q->>D: X1
  X->>Q: unlock()
  Q->>D: N1
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class atomic_rmw_seq extends uvm_sequence #(bus_item);
  `uvm_object_utils(atomic_rmw_seq)
  rand bit [31:0] addr;
  function new(string name = "atomic_rmw_seq"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    bus_item rd, wr;
    lock(m_sequencer);                    // grab(m_sequencer) for urgent traffic
    rd = bus_item::type_id::create("rd");
    start_item(rd); void'(rd.randomize() with { write == 0; addr == local::addr; }); finish_item(rd);
    get_response(rd);
    wr = bus_item::type_id::create("wr");
    start_item(wr); void'(wr.randomize() with { write == 1; addr == local::addr; data == rd.data | 1; }); finish_item(wr);
    unlock(m_sequencer);
  endtask
endclass
```
| | `lock` | `grab` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queue position | End | Front |
| Respects priority / other waiting sequences | Yes | No (bypasses them) |
| Blocked by an existing lock/grab | Yes | Yes |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Always release. Put `unlock` on every exit path, including early returns, or every other sequence starves.
- If the locking sequence is killed while holding the lock, the sequencer stays locked unless `stop_sequences()` is used.
- Without `get_response` support in the driver (`item_done(rsp)`), this read-modify-write example would hang.

### Follow-ups
- *Non-exclusive alternative?* Set the arbitration mode (`UVM_SEQ_ARB_STRICT_FIFO`) and a higher priority. That favors the sequence but does not guarantee back-to-back items.
artofverif-014:
**Key idea:** A **non-pipelined** driver handles one transaction at a time: `get_next_item`, drive the whole transfer, then `item_done`, so the sequence is blocked for the full duration. A **pipelined** driver lets the next request start before the previous one completes, as AXI/AHB address/data phase overlap requires. It accepts items early and finishes their later phases in parallel threads, returning responses with `put()` and response routing.

```wavedrom

  { "name": "clk",                 "wave": "p........." },
  {},
  { "name": "non-pipe addr",       "wave": "x3.x..4.x.", "data": ["A0","A1"] },
  { "name": "non-pipe data",       "wave": "x..3.x..4.", "data": ["D0","D1"] },
  {},
  { "name": "pipe addr",           "wave": "x34.5x....", "data": ["A0","A1","A2"] },
  { "name": "pipe data",           "wave": "x.345x....", "data": ["D0","D1","D2"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "pipelined: address of N+1 overlaps data of N" } }
```

### Explanation
**Non-pipelined**
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  forever begin
    seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
    drive_addr_phase(req);
    drive_data_phase(req);              // sequence is blocked all this time
    seq_item_port.item_done();
  end
endtask
```
**Pipelined (address and data phases as separate threads)**
```systemverilog
mailbox #(bus_item) data_q = new(2);   // depth bounds outstanding transfers

task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  fork
    addr_thread();
    data_thread();
  join
endtask

task addr_thread();
  forever begin
    seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
    drive_addr_phase(req);              // 1 cycle
    data_q.put(req);                    // hand to data thread
    seq_item_port.item_done();          // sequence may send next item now
  end
endtask

task data_thread();
  bus_item t, rsp;
  forever begin
    data_q.get(t);
    drive_data_phase(t);                // overlaps next address phase
    $cast(rsp, t.clone());
    rsp.set_id_info(t);
    seq_item_port.put(rsp);             // response routed by sequence id
  end
endtask
```
| | Non-pipelined | Pipelined |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outstanding transactions | 1 | N |
| `item_done` called | After full transfer | After request/address phase |
| Response path | `item_done(rsp)` or none | `put(rsp)` / `put_response`, matched by ID |
| Sequence side | `finish_item` = transfer done | `finish_item` = accepted; use `get_response` for completion |

- The sequence must consume responses (`get_response` or `use_response_handler(1)` with `response_handler`), or the response queue overflows.
- Bound the outstanding depth to match the protocol, or the driver accepts more items than the DUT allows.

### Follow-ups
- *How does the sequence wait for completion?* Call `get_response(rsp, req.get_transaction_id())` in a forked thread, or use the response handler.

**Key idea:** Every item carries the **sequence ID** of the sequence that sent it, plus a transaction ID. The driver must copy them into its response with **`rsp.set_id_info(req)`**. The sequencer then uses the sequence ID to put the response into the right sequence's response queue, where `get_response()` picks it up.

```mermaid
  participant B as seq B (id 7)

  B->>Q: req b (sequence_id 7)

  Q->>D: req b
  D->>Q: rsp with id 7
```

**Key idea:** **Early randomization** randomizes the item *before* `start_item()`, so the values are fixed before the sequence wins arbitration. **Late randomization** randomizes *after* `start_item()` returns, right before `finish_item()`.   participant Q as sequencer
```mermaid
  participant D as driver
  Note over S: EARLY
  S->>S: req.randomize()
  S->>Q: start_item(req) may wait many cycles
  Q-->>S: grant (values possibly stale)
  S->>Q: finish_item(req)
  Note over S: LATE
  S->>Q: start_item(req)
  Q-->>S: grant (driver is ready now)
  S->>S: req.randomize() with current state
  S->>Q: finish_item(req)
  Q->>D: req
```

```systemverilog

  req = item::type_id::create("req");
  if (!req.randomize()) `uvm_error("RND", "fail")
  start_item(req);                      // arbitration may take time
  finish_item(req);
endtask

// late (recommended)

  req = item::type_id::create("req");
  start_item(req);                      // granted: driver waiting
  if (!req.randomize() with { addr != last_addr; credit_ok == (p_sequencer.credits > 0); })
    `uvm_error("RND", "fail")
  finish_item(req);
  last_addr = req.addr;
endtask
```

| --- | --- | --- |
| When values are chosen | Before arbitration | After grant |
| Can react to current DUT/TB state | No, can be stale | Yes |
| Typical use | Pre-computing a list of items, checking constraints before requesting | Default for reactive and stateful stimulus |
| `` `uvm_do `` macros | — | Use late randomization |

- Never randomize *after* `finish_item`. The driver has already consumed the item.
- With late randomization, a randomization failure happens while holding the grant. Report it and still call `finish_item` (or handle the failure) so the driver does not stall.

```mermaid
  participant D as driver

  D->>Q: item_done()
  Q-->>S: finish_item returns
```

**Key idea:** **Blocking:** `get()`, `get_next_item()`, `peek()`, which wait until an item exists. **Non-blocking:** `item_done()` (a function), `try_next_item()` (does not wait for an item; only delta-cycle waits) and `put()` (never waits in practice, since the response queue is not bounded by back-pressure).

| `peek(req)` | task | Yes | **Blocking** |
| `try_next_item(req)` | task | No: returns `null` if nothing ready (may wait delta cycles) | **Non-blocking** |
| `item_done(rsp = null)` | function | No | **Non-blocking** |
| `put(rsp)` | task | No in practice (calls `put_response` immediately) | **Non-blocking** |
| `put_response(rsp)` | function | No | Non-blocking |
| `has_do_available()` | function | No | Non-blocking |

**Key idea:** Call `sequencer.stop_sequences()`. It kills every sequence (and child sequence) running on that sequencer and clears the arbitration queue and locks. The driver may still hold an item in flight, so it must be resynchronized too: finish or abandon the current item without calling `item_done` on a dead sequence. Typically you kill and restart the driver thread around the reset.

```mermaid
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant S as running sequences
  participant D as driver

  Q->>S: kill() all, clear queues and locks

  T->>D: restart run thread after reset
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog

task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  forever begin
    @(negedge vif.rst_n);            // wait for reset assertion
    fork
      begin : main
        @(posedge vif.rst_n);        // wait for reset release
        forever begin
          seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
          drive(req);
          seq_item_port.item_done();
        end
      end
      @(negedge vif.rst_n);          // next reset kills main
    join_any
    disable fork;
    drive_idle();
  end
endtask

// test / env on reset
task handle_reset();
  env.agt.sqr.stop_sequences();      // kill all sequences on this sequencer
endtask
```

**Key idea:** `build_phase` constructs the hierarchy, and a component can only be built after its parent has created it. Execution must therefore start at the root (`uvm_test_top`) and move **down**.   participant E as env
```mermaid
  participant A as agent
  participant D as driver

  E->>E: build_phase: get env_cfg
  E->>A: create("agt", this)
  A->>A: build_phase: get is_active
  A->>D: create("drv", this) if ACTIVE
  D->>D: build_phase: get vif
```

- **Existence:** before `test.build_phase` runs, `env` is just a null handle. The phase engine can only call `env.build_phase` once the test has created the env, so the traversal follows creation from the root downwards.
- **Configuration:** parents set `config_db` entries targeted at their subtree before creating children, so children always see the right config when they `get` it.
- **Overrides:** factory overrides from the test are in place before any lower-level `create()` call.

**Key idea:** `phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase)` is a component callback that UVM calls when a task phase's objections all drop, **before** the phase actually ends. A component that still has work (a scoreboard waiting for in-flight transactions, a background sequence to stop) can **re-raise** an objection there to extend the phase, then drop it when finished. The callback can run again, up to 20 iterations by default.

```mermaid
  participant T as test
  participant P as run_phase
  participant S as scoreboard
  T->>P: drop_objection (count 0)
  P->>S: phase_ready_to_end(phase)
  S->>P: raise_objection (exp queue not empty)
  S->>S: wait until exp queue empty
  S->>P: drop_objection
  P->>S: phase_ready_to_end again
  S-->>P: nothing pending
  P->>P: phase ends, go to extract
```

```systemverilog
  pkt exp_q[$];
  virtual function void phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase);
    if (phase.get_name() != "run") return;
    if (exp_q.size() != 0) begin
      phase.raise_objection(this, "waiting for outstanding packets");
      fork
        begin
          wait (exp_q.size() == 0);
          phase.drop_objection(this, "drained");
        end
      join_none
    end
  endfunction
endclass
```

- It is a **function**. Waiting must happen in a forked process, as shown.
- If no objection is re-raised, the phase ends immediately after the callback.
